body: Wednesday, December 17 2025 — Macro · Sectors · Flows · Crypto

Macro Stance: Mixed. The labour data that reached the market on December 16 show a slowing employment base inside a still-growing economy: payrolls rose by 64,000 in November after falling by 105,000 in October, and the unemployment rate reached a four-year high even as jobs were added. Activity is softer at the margin, with business growth in December at a six-month low and the November ISM manufacturing index at 48.2%, still in contraction. The Fed has already delivered a third cut this year, Collins called the latest cut a ‘close call’, and Williams said policy is in a good position with inflation moderating in 2026. The working read is a Fed on hold after three cuts, with the next move set by late-arriving data and by a leadership change that the market is still pricing.

Rates & Curve: On the US Treasury par curve at the prior close, the 2-year yield was 3.48% and the 10-year 4.15%, a 10Y−2Y spread of 67 bps; the 3-month was 3.64% and the 30-year 4.82% (US Treasury, prior close 2025-12-16). Over 20 observations the 2-year fell 12 bps while the 10-year rose 2 bps, so the spread widened by 14 bps; the card classes the curve as moderately steep, approaching the long-run average, and the move as steepening (10Y up, 2Y down/flat) (US Treasury, prior close 2025-12-16). Over five observations the 2-year fell 13 bps and the 10-year fell 3 bps, so the long end has not followed the front end in the last week. Treasury yields edged lower after the jobs figures, which is a front-end move; the long end is being held up by supply and term premium, which the feed does not measure, so that part of the reading is ours. Equities did not confirm a growth scare: the S&P 500 closed at 6,800.26, down 0.24% in the prior session and up 1.92% over 20 sessions, with the VIX at 16.48 after a 26.36% fall over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). The dollar index stood at 98.15, down 1.45% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16).

New / Most Important: The most important new fact is the delayed November jobs report. A Reuters explainer dated December 15 listed the delayed employment and CPI reports as due in the same week, with gaps in the data, and a Morningstar piece on the shutdown-affected November CPI report points to inflation as the next print the market will read. Congress is also a source of event risk: a House panel set a vote on paying air traffic controllers during shutdowns, and senators are bracing for another possible shutdown in January. On the Fed’s leadership, the WSJ reports Trump will interview the Fed’s Christopher Waller for the chair, CNBC quotes Hassett saying Fed independence is ‘really important’, and Fortune reports a new chair could be announced before Christmas. A Dallas Fed paper argues that the transmission of the funds rate is weakening, which limits how much another cut can do for the real economy.

Playbook ✓: Stay neutral on duration overall and express any view in the belly of the curve. The 2-year fell 12 bps over 20 sessions while the 10-year rose 2 bps, so the steepening is a front-end story; buy 2-year exposure on a soft November CPI print and cut it if core inflation surprises higher. Keep equity exposure near index weight, but buy protection while it is cheap: a VIX at 16.48 after a 26.36% fall over 20 sessions is not pricing a shock, so index puts are inexpensive insurance against a leadership-change episode (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). What would change the call: a CPI print that confirms weakness would extend the front-end rally, while a chair choice that the market reads as a threat to Fed independence would lift the long end and the term premium, which is where the curve would steepen further.

Macro Stance: Mixed. The end-of-year data describe a euro area that is resilient but slow. Business activity expanded in November at the fastest pace in 30 months on the PMI, yet the December flash surveys show French private-sector growth slowing to a crawl and German manufacturing contracting again. The ECB is on hold: inflation ticked up to 2.2% in November on the flash estimate, and Lagarde said on December 12 that the bank may lift its growth outlook again. The working read is a steady ECB with an activity gap between services and manufacturing that the bank will not close by cutting.

Activity & Inflation: Euro-area inflation rose to 2.2% in November on the flash estimate, which keeps the ECB on hold. Activity is the weak spot: Germany’s economy is stuck in the slow lane according to economic institutes, and the Mittelstand has lost faith in the government’s ability to revive the economy. The December flash PMI showed French private-sector growth slowing to a crawl. Credit conditions are the offset: the ECB proposed simpler bank regulation but rejected calls for lower capital buffers, and Euronews reports European banks had their best year on record. The euro is the transmission channel: EUR/USD closed at 1.1755, up 1.42% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16), so a weaker dollar is already doing part of the easing.

New / Most Important: The largest policy change in the window is the EU’s retreat from the 2035 combustion-engine ban. Reuters reports the EU drops the 2035 ban as the global EV shift faces a reset, the Commission is described as killing its flagship combustion-engine ban, and Volkswagen welcomed the move. Stellantis said the EU proposals fall short of the industry’s energy-transition needs. Separately, the EU imposed sanctions on oil traders linked to Russia’s shipping network, which keeps energy-trade compliance on the agenda for banks and traders.

Playbook ✓: Keep the euro-area equity overweight concentrated in banks rather than autos into year-end. STOXX Europe 600 closed at 579.80, up 3.19% over 20 sessions, and the DAX at 24,076.87, up 3.87% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). Hold the euro exposure at half a hedge, since EUR/USD has already rallied 1.42% over 20 sessions and the ECB is not offering a catalyst for a further move. The trigger to change the call is a German or French flash PMI that recovers toward the November pace, which would lift cyclicals; a policy shock from the ECB or a reversal of the auto policy would change the view on autos.

Macro Stance: Bearish on domestic demand. Policy promises have not yet reached households or property, and the hard data show the economy losing momentum. Industrial output grew 4.8% in November while retail sales rose 1.3%, and CNBC reported that retail growth sharply missed estimates, deepening consumption worries. Reuters said the economy stalled in November as calls for reform grow, and the SCMP reports that growth engines sputter as retail and investment are hit. Markets confirm the read: the Shanghai Composite closed at 3,824.81, down 2.92% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16).

PMIs & Activity: The feed carries no fresh official manufacturing or services PMI for December, so the latest available hard print is the November activity data released on 14 December. The November private services PMI slipped to a five-month low, and the November activity figures show industrial output growing while retail and investment slowed. Investment is the weak link: the New York Times describes a historic shift underway as the investment slump deepens, and Money.pl reports China recorded its first fall in investment in decades. Steel output is set to slump to a seven-year low as iron-ore imports hit a record. What would confirm the view is a December activity print where retail sales do not regain the November pace while steel output keeps falling.

Credit Impulse: Credit is not accelerating. Bloomberg reports that China’s credit expansion stays muted as demand languishes, and a Caixin analysis warns that bad-debt managers’ bets on bank stocks could backfire. Shadow banking is back in the spotlight after the earlier debt crackdown. Policy has signalled help: the government vowed a flexible rate and reserve-requirement cuts to boost the economy in 2026, and Caixin reports that the 2026 priorities centre on demand revival. The feed carries no November new-loan figure, so the credit impulse cannot be measured directly here. A new-loan print that stays weak after an RRR cut would confirm that the easing has not yet reached borrowers.

Property: Property remains the drag that policy has not reversed. Home prices slid further in November, and a Reuters poll expects prices to fall 3.7% this year and extend declines into 2026. The developer Vanke sits at the centre of the risk: bondholders rejected a payment extension, raising default risk, and an analyst warned it was on the brink of default as bailout hopes faded. Bloomberg reports that Vanke lost support from a key state-owned shareholder and that its last ‘too-big-to-fail’ housing giant has lost state support. Authorities vow stability, but the market has not seen a rescue. A Vanke payment decision that pushes losses onto bondholders would confirm the view; a state-backed rescue would be the first sign of a policy floor under developers.

Fiscal, Policy & Trade: Fiscal policy is promised, not yet shown. China promised a fiscal boost next year and recognised a ‘prominent’ imbalance, and the IMF urged bolder stimulus and a shift away from relying on exports. The trade side runs against domestic weakness: the surplus topped $1 trillion for the first time, growing on non-US demand, with exports up 5.9% in November while shipments to the US dropped 29%. Mexico’s Senate approved tariff hikes on Chinese and other Asian imports, and Mexico stands by its decision for 50% tariffs on Chinese goods. China cut anti-dumping duties on EU pork in its final ruling after an 18-month probe, a sign of selective trade détente with Europe.

Markets & Flows: The Shanghai Composite closed at 3,824.81 in the prior session, down 1.11% that day and 2.92% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). The Hang Seng closed at 25,235.41, down 1.54% in the prior session and 2.68% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). ASHR, the CSI 300 A-share ETF, was essentially flat over 20 sessions at 32.53 after a 0.97% fall in the prior session, while KWEB, the China internet ETF, fell 4.69% over 20 sessions to 36.15 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). USD/CNY closed at 7.0470, down 0.85% over 20 sessions, a firmer yuan (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). Bloomberg reports Chinese stocks are set for a correction as the rally fades on a weak economy, while Hong Kong stocks rallied on property hopes earlier in the month.

New / Most Important: The most important new item is Vanke’s bond rejection, because it tests whether state support holds for property. Alongside it, China’s chip listings are running hot: MetaX rose nearly 700% in its Shanghai debut, and Biren’s Hong Kong IPO received Beijing’s go-ahead. The yuan is part of the debate as well: the SCMP expects the currency to break a key dollar level in 2026, and Goldman Sachs says the yuan is 25% undervalued on a trade basis. The yuan trend is the one market signal that does not confirm the weak-economy story.

Playbook ✓: Underweight domestic-demand equities, Hong Kong property and mainland consumer names until the credit data turn, with KWEB as the short or hedge vehicle rather than the broad Asia index, because KWEB has already fallen 4.69% over 20 sessions and the internet names carry the policy risk (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). Prefer onshore yuan exposure as the cleaner expression of a weak-growth, no-devaluation view, since USD/CNY is already lower over 20 sessions. The trigger to change the call is a new-loan print that accelerates after the RRR cut, or a state-backed Vanke rescue. ⚠ Divergence: MetaX rose nearly 700% on its Shanghai debut while the macro prints weaken, so the market is paying for a technology theme rather than for the domestic economy.

Macro Stance: Mixed, with a yen-supportive bias. The Bank of Japan is set to raise its benchmark rate to the highest level since 1995, and Reuters describes the move as taking rates to a 30-year high. A Reuters exclusive of December 12 said the BOJ would pledge more rate hikes at its policy meeting, and Japan’s business mood hit a four-year high, keeping the rate-hike view alive. The working read is that the policy move is widely expected and that the yen trade is already partly in the price.

Activity & Currency: Exports grew at the fastest pace in nine months, sharply beating expectations, and the manufacturing PMI contracted at a slower pace in December. The yen outperforms G-10 peers on growing BOJ rate-hike bets. USD/JPY closed at 155.0150, down 0.17% over 20 sessions and 0.56% in the prior session (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). The Nikkei 225 closed at 49,383.29, down 1.87% over 20 sessions and 1.56% in the prior session (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). On the fiscal side, Japan passed an extra budget to fund its biggest post-COVID stimulus and is weighing an income-tax hike from 2027 to help fund defence. Investors are worried about the bond market, and the BOJ is said to start selling ETF holdings as soon as January.

Playbook ✓: Stay long the yen against the dollar into the hike, but size it for a sell-the-news reaction, since USD/JPY has fallen only 0.17% over 20 sessions and the move is not yet fully priced (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). Hedge the Nikkei long with yen exposure rather than dollars. The trigger to change the call is BOJ guidance that signals a pause, which would unwind the yen-carry positioning; the Seeking Alpha headline on a carry unwind is the risk to watch. A tax headline that lifts long JGB yields would weaken the yen case, so track the yield move alongside the policy decision.

Macro Stance: Bullish on the Australian dollar, with a tightening bias at the RBA. The central bank kept its rate at 3.6% and flagged rate-hike risk as it ended its brief easing cycle. Two of the big four banks now see a hike in February, and Commonwealth Bank and NAB made the same call in their 2026 outlook. Consumer inflation accelerated to 3.8% in October, overshooting estimates, and the Guardian reports markets now price a hike in 2026. The working read is that the RBA-Fed divergence is supporting the currency.

Demand & Financing: Demand is mixed. Australia’s November jobs fell by the most in nine months while the unemployment rate held steady, and annual growth hit a two-year high in the third quarter. The government was forced to lift its inflation forecast while keeping its spending plans intact, which adds to the case for a tighter RBA. For borrowers, a big bank hiked twice in a month as 12 lenders lifted rates. AUD/USD closed at 0.6642, up 2.3% over 20 sessions and down 0.08% in the prior session (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). The S&P/ASX 200 closed at 8,598.90, up 1.53% over 20 sessions and down 0.42% in the prior session (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16).

Playbook ✓: Own AUD against the USD on pullbacks while the RBA-Fed rate divergence persists; the trigger is the next monthly CPI, and a print at the current inflation pace keeps the February hike in the banks’ forecasts. Prefer miners as the rate-hike hedge for domestic equities, since a Macquarie view says mining stocks are the best way to play hikes in 2026. The risk to the call is labour: job losses could give the RBA ‘pause for thought’ on hikes, which would take the currency lower. What would change the call is a jobs print that weakens further, which would move the banks’ hike forecasts out of the first half.

Monetary & Activity: Bankier reports core inflation fell below 3% for the first time in six years, and Rzeczpospolita says every measure of core inflation in Poland is down, at the lowest readings in years. The central bank cut rates for the sixth time this year, and Parkiet argues the cycle of cuts is nearing its end. November inflation was exactly at the NBP target, the statistics office revised its first estimate. The budget is under pressure: the deficit reached 245 billion zloty after November, and forecasts point to a record NBP loss. A Business Insider Polska headline calls the pillar of Polish GDP accelerating a positive surprise, so activity is not the weak link.

FX & Markets: USD/PLN closed at 3.5871, down 1.79% over 20 sessions, and EUR/PLN at 4.2163, down 0.40% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). The iShares MSCI Poland ETF, EPOL, closed at 34.41, up 3.05% over 20 sessions after a 4.15% fall in the prior session (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). The WIG20 total-return tracker, ETFBW20TR, closed at 61.81, up 7.01% over 20 sessions and down 1.07% in the prior session (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). Among named stocks, LPP closed at 20,370.00 zloty, up 28.11% over 20 sessions, KGH at 253.70, up 34.23%, PKO at 82.82, up 12.59%, PZU at 66.86, up 13.25%, and PEO at 208.60, up 11.16% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). PGE closed at 8.55, down 15.62% over 20 sessions, and PKN at 91.90, down 8.76%, the laggards (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). A wnp.pl headline says the zloty has moved in a way not seen for seven years.

Companies: LPP is the test case. An Investing.com headline calls LPP shares the most expensive in its history, yet the company posted a Q3 net loss of 18 million zloty even as adjusted EBITDA reached 1.7 billion zloty. Dino Polska fell below 40 zloty, and analysts call it an opportunity for 2026, while a collective labour dispute has started at the chain. PGE’s chief executive change raised questions about what went wrong, and PGE’s shares are the weakest of the named stocks in the card, down 15.62% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). Orlen sold 2 billion zloty of corporate bonds to fund investment and is refunding money tied to its takeover of Grupa Azoty. KGHM signed an agreement with a Canadian First Nation for the Victoria mine development.

Security & New Development: Security spending is turning into industrial orders. Germany is sending troops to Poland to bolster eastern flank defences, and Poland is boosting civil defence after Russian provocations. Poland received all 212 South Korean K9 self-propelled howitzers and took delivery of the first 15 Borsuk tanks. The offshore wind auction is seen as a key test for Europe after failed tenders. JSW needs more than 830 million dollars to stay afloat, the minister says, a reminder that the heavy industry names are a different story from the consumer names.

Playbook ✓: Overweight the WIG20 total-return tracker into year-end for its bank-heavy exposure, but do not chase LPP at record levels. Keep the zloty hedged on the euro leg, since USD/PLN is already down 1.79% over 20 sessions and EUR/PLN is flat-to-lower (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). Trigger to change the call: a cut-cycle signal from the central bank that lands later than the Parkiet view, or a fiscal decision that widens the deficit beyond the 245 billion zloty already reported. ⚠ Divergence: LPP posted a Q3 net loss of 18 million zloty while its share price is at a record, so the price is running ahead of earnings.

Narrative: Technology is split between AI spending and AI payback. The sector ETF closed at 142.56, up 0.52% over 20 sessions and down 3.69% over five (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). Barron’s says chip stocks are in a bubble but ‘here’s more good news’, while Yahoo says Nvidia and Broadcom are Wall Street’s top chip picks for 2026. The driver that matters now is whether hyperscaler capex is disciplined; CNBC says AI spending could slow down if Oracle shows discipline.

Reported: Oracle’s revenue forecast missed Wall Street targets while spending rose, and the shares slid about 10%; the stock fell 12% despite an earnings beat as a $50 billion spending plan stunned investors. Broadcom beat on earnings and revenue and said its AI chip sales would double in the current quarter, but the shares fell on margin pressure. Adobe reported record fourth-quarter revenue, and Synopsys reported its fiscal-year results.

EPS Upside Watch: Micron is the clearest set-up. UBS raised its Micron target heading into the company’s results, which a CNBC headline placed in the following week, and Barron’s highlights soaring memory-chip prices. The caution is that rising chip costs will push smartphone shipments down in 2026. Micron closed at 232.51, down 3.90% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16), so the expectations reset has already happened in the price.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The convention is that AI beats lift the group, but Broadcom shows beats being sold when margins are the problem. Nvidia closed at 177.72, down 4.76% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16), and Seeking Alpha calls for a big decline. The signal that cuts the other way is Nvidia buying SchedMD to push its open-source AI stack, which keeps the platform narrative intact.

Narrative: Communication services is a mix of ad-funded platforms and streaming. XLC closed at 116.65, up 4.92% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). Meta closed at 657.15, up 9.16% over 20 sessions, and Alphabet at 306.57, up 7.56% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). The narrative is ad strength; the driver is AI monetisation, and the feed flags the platform risk that ad fraud is being tolerated to protect revenue.

Reported: Netflix has announced the date of its fourth-quarter 2025 results. Disney’s shares are up 5.61% over 20 sessions to 111.62 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16), and a billion-dollar OpenAI deal lets users make content with Disney characters, a new revenue channel the feed reports without a price.

EPS Upside Watch: Netflix is the set-up. The shares closed at 94.57, down 14.25% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16), after a selloff that Bloomberg puts at $40 billion, and the fourth-quarter results are the test. The bull case is that a quality subscription name is cheap into a results date; the bear case is the debt load that Bloomberg frames as ‘Debtflix’.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The convention says Netflix is a defensive growth name, so the selloff should not be happening. Its 20-session drop is larger than any other communication-services name in the card, which breaks the defensive narrative. The writer’s reading is that the market is charging for the debt and the content spend rather than for the subscriber base.

Narrative: Financials have the best 20-session momentum among the cyclicals. XLF closed at 54.64, up 6.20% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). Goldman Sachs rose 13.36% over the same window to 879.15 and JPMorgan 5.05% to 315.55 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). The narrative is capital-markets strength and a steeper curve; the driver is the US bank rally the card already shows, which the Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan moves above reflect; as a labelled European read-across, Reuters says the AI boom is supercharging European banks’ rally.

Reported: Citigroup’s turnaround progress won a thumbs-up from JPMorgan. HSBC’s $13.6 billion buyout proposal for Hang Seng Bank won the nod of the bank’s board committee. Visa launched stablecoin settlement for US banks in Circle’s USDC, and Walmart and other retailers objected to the Visa and Mastercard settlement.

EPS Upside Watch: The curve is the earnings tailwind. The 10Y−2Y spread widened by 14 bps over 20 sessions on the Treasury curve (US Treasury, prior close 2025-12-16), which supports net interest margins. Asset-based finance is growing, with Pimco gathering $7 billion for a new strategy, and fee income from that activity is the upside the sector is set up to capture.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The signal that cuts against the bank narrative is the shadow-banking growth. The FSB says shadow banking is growing at double the rate of traditional lenders, and Morningstar DBRS expects private-credit pressures to fuel further defaults in 2026. The writer’s reading is that the lending growth the banks are chasing carries the default risk that the regulator is flagging.

Narrative: Energy is in a supply-glut narrative. XLE closed at 43.81, down 3.01% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). WTI closed at 55.27, down 7.74% over 20 sessions, and Brent at 58.92, down 8.22% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). The driver is the surplus: US crude closed at its lowest level since early 2021 as a looming surplus weighed on the market, and oil fell to a four-year low below $55.

Reported: The feed carries no recent energy earnings. Cheniere fell as LNG stocks came under pressure, and Russia’s oil and gas revenue is poised to hit its lowest level since August 2020. Venezuela’s oil exports fell sharply after the US tanker seizure, a supply shock the market is not pricing as a supply loss.

EPS Upside Watch: Few upside surprises are set up for producers in a glut. The exception is tanker rates, which Reuters expects to stay strong into 2026 as sanctions remove ships for hire. Exxon closed at 114.68, down 2.55% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16), so the upside would have to come from cost discipline rather than from price.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The IEA lowered its 2026 oil glut forecast for the first time since May, and OPEC data indicate a close oil supply-demand balance in 2026 with no glut. China is stepping up crude stockpiling, a demand offset to the surplus story. The writer’s reading is that the glut is consensus while the forecasters and the stockpile data disagree on its size.

Narrative: Industrials are rallying on infrastructure and power demand. XLI closed at 156.06, up 3.68% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). Caterpillar closed at 588.93, up 6.68% over 20 sessions, and Boeing at 206.71, up 7.77% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). The narrative is energy-driven capex; the driver now is whether equipment demand holds after the Deere call that 2026 is the bottom.

Reported: Caterpillar rode energy growth past estimates, and Deere called 2026 the bottom of its cycle in the same report. CNBC’s week-ahead preview put FedEx and Jabil’s earnings on the calendar. Spirit and Frontier Airlines are reported to be eyeing a merger, and Frontier replaced its longtime CEO.

EPS Upside Watch: The defence set-up is mixed. Morgan Stanley says defence stocks offer attractive value heading into 2026, but the Trump administration is targeting shareholder payouts at defence giants as cost overruns mount. Defence shares have also been sold on Ukraine peace progress, so the upside in this group depends on the budget, not on the geopolitical premium.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The convention is that geopolitical tension lifts defence. Defence stocks fell as the Ukraine talks progressed, which is the opposite of the trade the convention implies. The signal that matters is the pressure on payouts, which the market is listening to even as the value case holds.

Narrative: Consumer discretionary is a tale of two stories. XLY closed at 121.93, up 6.62% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16), while consumer sentiment is weak: CNBC says consumers feel gloomy about the economy but keep spending, and Stocktwits says even Wall Street admits the American shopper is tapped out. The driver is the tension between spending and sentiment.

Reported: Ford is taking a $19.5 billion charge as it pulls back on EV plans. US retail sales were unexpectedly unchanged in October, with a drop in motor-vehicle purchases behind the stall. Lululemon’s stock popped on an earnings beat and CEO change, and Macy’s rose 9.1% after raising guidance.

EPS Upside Watch: The holiday data point to strength. Reuters reports record shoppers and an online sales surge signal strong US holiday momentum, and Black Friday online sales hit $8.6 billion, according to Adobe Analytics. Tesla shares rose on confirmed driverless robotaxi testing, and the card has Tesla at 489.88, up 19.80% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16).

⚡ Breaking Convention: The convention is that holiday strength lifts discretionary names together. Amazon fell 4.43% over 20 sessions to 222.56 and Home Depot 1.49% to 352.68 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16), while Tesla rose on robotaxi news. The writer’s reading is that the sector is trading on single-name catalysts rather than on the consumer.

Narrative: Staples are rising modestly. XLP closed at 79.28, up 3.27% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). Walmart closed at 115.42, up 12.11% over 20 sessions, and formally relocated its listing to the Nasdaq. The narrative is the defensive value bid, with the driver being low-income trade-down; dollar stores are seeing higher-income shoppers too.

Reported: Costco beat quarterly earnings estimates on strong demand, with comparable sales growth of 6.4%, but the stock ticked lower on the print. Costco closed at 860.39, down 5.72% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16).

EPS Upside Watch: The set-up favours staples with traffic growth. The holiday-season surveys point to strength in online and value channels, and a membership warehouse with a comparable-sales beat is the clearest example. The risk is that the beat is already in the price, as the Costco print shows.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The convention is that staples are defensive. Costco beat and fell, which shows the defensive premium is fading at the high-multiple end of the group. The writer’s reading is that staples are now a valuation trade rather than a safe-haven trade.

Narrative: Health care is up 1.56% over 20 sessions to 154.07 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). Eli Lilly rose 3.19% over 20 sessions to 1,054.29 and UnitedHealth 4.27% to 334.20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-12-16). The narrative is a biotech rebound: Fierce Biotech says biotech is poised to outperform the bear markets of 2021 to 2024. The driver is pricing policy, which the drug-affordability headlines keep in view.
